demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one', the body-focused appraisals 'I can no longer trust my own body' and 'I feel ashamed of what happened to my body' are hard to reconcile clinically unless the patient also directly experienced major bodily violation/injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

The memory items imply vivid sensory reliving of the traumatic event ('hear things ... heard during the frightening event') and fragmented visual snapshots, which can occur in PTSD, but here they are not well matched to the selected appraisals: the profile centers on bodily shame/unreliability rather than grief/death-related meanings of the event.

'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' is not impossible, but in this profile it appears weakly integrated: there are no trigger or threat items tying work contexts to the trauma, and the formulation does not include trigger/threat pathways. The coping profile otherwise concerns sleep delay and undereating, so work avoidance feels insufficiently anchored.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, body-focused shame is clinically hard to reconcile unless there was also direct bodily violation, injury, or assault. The rest of the profile centers grief-related loss, meaning, and intrusive memory phenomena, so this item appears inconsistent with the trauma type and with the other selected items.

vignette:
Maya, a 46-year-old forensic analyst from New Zealand, had always prided herself on her analytical mind and sharp attention to detail. She loved her job, which involved piecing together evidence in complex criminal cases, but everything changed when her younger sister, Leila, died unexpectedly in a car accident. The news hit her like a freight train, tearing through the fabric of her life with brutal force. Leila had been her closest confidante, the one person with whom she shared her hopes and fears. In the aftermath of the tragedy, Maya found herself grappling not only with grief but also with a profound sense of disconnection from the world around her.

In the weeks that followed Leila's death, Maya experienced a shift in her ability to function. The once-reliable structure of her daily routine became unrecognizable. She would sit at her desk, staring blankly at the case files in front of her, but her mind was elsewhere, consumed by haunting snapshots of the accident—images of twisted metal and flashing lights, moments that felt frozen in time. During these episodes, she would hear echoes of the sirens blaring, a sound that reverberated in her mind long after it had faded from the scene. The auditory recall was relentless, pulling her back into the depths of despair each time she tried to focus on her work. What frightened Maya most was how easily these memories could overwhelm her, leaving her breathless and teetering on the edge of an emotional precipice.

As days turned into weeks, Maya found herself avoiding work altogether. She would tell her supervisor that she needed personal days to grieve, but in truth, she felt unable to bear the thought of facing her colleagues or the cases she used to find so engaging. Each time she thought about returning, she felt a heavy weight in her chest, an instinct that screamed at her to stay away. This avoidance not only eroded her professional identity but also strained her relationship with her husband, David. He was supportive, but she could see the worry etched on his face as he watched her retreat further into herself. Their conversations grew shorter, often overshadowed by Maya's silence, and the laughter they once shared became a distant memory.

Maya's coping mechanisms took an unhealthy turn. Nights were spent tossing and turning, her mind racing with thoughts of her sister and the life that had been ripped away. To cope, she began delaying sleep, staying up until the early hours of the morning, scrolling through old photos of Leila on her phone, desperately trying to grasp at the memories. Each image felt like a double-edged sword, bringing both comfort and unbearable pain. As her sleep deprivation deepened, she also found herself losing her appetite. Meals became a chore, and she often skipped breakfast or lunch, telling herself that eating felt meaningless when everything else in her life had crumbled.

Maya had come to believe that nothing held any significance anymore. She felt as if her life had been irrevocably destroyed by the trauma. The laughter of children playing outside her window felt like a cruel reminder of what she had lost, and the vibrant colors of life seemed muted, devoid of joy. The faith she once had in the goodness of people and the beauty of life began to fade, replaced by a pervasive sense of hopelessness. She felt like a ghost in her own existence, trapped in a world that no longer made sense.

It wasn’t until a particularly challenging day at work, when a case involving a young girl’s tragic death resurfaced, that Maya finally hit her breaking point. The auditory memories returned with a vengeance, and the emotional weight became too much to bear. In that moment, she realized she could not continue down this path. She felt utterly lost, and for the first time, she acknowledged that she needed help. It was this moment of clarity that led her to seek therapy, hoping to find a way to navigate the tumultuous waters of her grief and reclaim some semblance of meaning in her life. Maya was terrified of facing the deep pain that lay ahead but also held a flicker of hope that healing might be possible. What she longed for most was to rediscover the joy in everyday moments and, perhaps, to feel connected to the world once more.
